wine.name: Hamilton Russell Vineyards Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, close to the cold Atlantic at Hermanus, on stony, clay rich, low vigour soils derived from Bokkeveld shale.
wine.making: Made only from the estate's own Pinot Noir, the wine goes through its malolactic conversion in full and is aged about ten months in 228 litre French oak barrels, about a third to nearly half of them new in the house's sheets, before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and raspberry over forest floor and a savoury, earthy note that can make it seem backward in youth; juicy acidity and fine grained tannin, more structure and savour than sweetness of fruit.
wine.ageing: Often closed and earthy for its first few years, it opens with five or more in bottle and keeps well beyond a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's own name, kept for its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay alone.
The Wine of Origin ward nearest the sea of the three that bear the Hemel-en-Aarde name.

records.table: Stony, clay rich shale in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley behind Hermanus, close to the cold sea, gives Hamilton Russell Vineyards its Pinot Noir. Savoury and fine grained rather than sweet, a young bottle opens with air and a cool pour.
records.story: In 1975 an advertising executive bought a run down, undeveloped property in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley behind Hermanus, a place then almost unknown for wine. Vines went in from 1976, and by Bouchard Finlayson's own timeline the valley's first modern cellar was built on the farm that year. The first vintage came in 1981: its Pinot Noir, from young vines, was labelled Grand Vin Noir, and by Decanter's account the first Chardonnay followed in 1982. In 1991 the founder's son took over and narrowed the estate to two grapes alone, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and in 1994 he bought the property from the family, keeping the vines on the stony, clay rich shale that suits them. The family's wines of other grapes went out under other names, Southern Right from 1994 and Ashbourne from 1996, so the house's own name stays on those two. The founder died in 2013. The valley it pioneered became a Wine of Origin ward in its own right, and Bouchard Finlayson, whose founding winemaker had made the early wines here, and Newton Johnson followed it into the Hemel-en-Aarde. The Pinot Noir is the wine that showed, in the 1980s, that South Africa could grow Pinot Noir of savoury depth beside a cold sea.

wine.name: Galpin Peak Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The estate's Pinot Noir vineyards beneath Galpin Peak in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, densely planted on ancient, stony, clay rich Bokkeveld shale, shallow soils that keep the vines' vigour low.
wine.making: Aged about eleven months in French oak barrels, under a third of them new by the house's sheets, then given about four months more of élevage before bottling. In the strongest years chosen barrels are set aside as the Tête de Cuvée.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and plum with clove and a touch of violet, turning smoky and savoury as it matures; a light frame of oak, fine tannin and a long, firm finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage, it gains savour for a decade and more, and the house's own sheets give it at least eight years.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The fynbos covered mountain above the vineyards, which gives the Pinot Noir its name.

records.table: Galpin Peak is Bouchard Finlayson's Pinot Noir, named for the mountain above its vineyards in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, a house founded with a Burgundian partner in 1989. Grown on stony shale and clay, it tastes of red cherry, raspberry and clove, firm and fine.
records.story: Bouchard Finlayson was set up in 1989 as a partnership between a Burgundian winemaker of the Bouchard family and a Cape winemaker who had made the early wines at Hamilton Russell next door, where by the house's own timeline he had built the valley's first modern winery in 1976. The two set out to make Pinot Noir in the Burgundian manner, densely planted, and the first vines on the new estate went in during 1989. The first vintage followed in 1991. The Pinot Noir took the name of Galpin Peak, the fynbos covered mountain of about 810 metres that, with the higher Tower of Babel, shelters the valley. In 2000 the estate was bought by a family of hoteliers, and the Cape winemaker stayed on as cellar master, later handing the making of the wine to a successor. From chosen barrels of the strongest years the house bottles a Tête de Cuvée apart, while Hannibal, a red blend of Italian and French grapes, shows the partners' wider curiosity. Galpin Peak is the house's answer to Burgundy on Cape shale: Pinot Noir from dense plantings on shallow, stony clay beneath a mountain, made to last.

wine.name: Family Vineyards Pinot Noir
wine.appellation: Wine of Origin Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the family's own vineyards.
wine.sites: Several of the family's own parcels in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, a few kilometres from the Atlantic, the Mrs M and Windansea vineyards among them, on decomposed granite over iron rich clay.
wine.making: Each parcel is fermented apart with its own wild yeasts, a share of it as whole bunches that varies from site to site and year to year, and stays about 25 days on its skins. The wine is then aged about eleven months in 228 litre barrels made in Burgundy, under a third of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Violet and rose petal over red cherry and wild strawberry, with a faint note of fynbos; fresh, lively acidity and fine tannin, perfumed and light on its feet rather than heavy.
wine.ageing: Charming within a few years of the vintage, it keeps its perfume and gains savour for eight to ten years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: Made only from the parcels the family farms itself, blended together.

records.table: Newton Johnson's Family Vineyards Pinot Noir blends the family's own parcels on decomposed granite in the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, a few kilometres from the Atlantic. It smells of violet, rose and red cherry and stays fresh and fine, so serve it cool.
records.story: Newton Johnson joins two family names. In 1995 a Cape Wine Master, who had written his thesis on Pinot Noir, and his wife, born a Newton, moved to the Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and built a cellar before they planted any vines; the Newton side, the house says, traces its roots to Falkirk in Scotland. The first vintage, in 1997, was made from bought in fruit. The family planted its first Pinot Noir on its own farm around 2003, by the house's account, on decomposed granite over clay a few kilometres from the sea, and the founders' sons came to lead the house in the cellar and the vines. The first Family Vineyards Pinot Noir came with the 2008 vintage, drawn by the house's sheet from the Seadragon vineyard alone, and as the younger vineyards matured more parcels joined it. Single vineyards, Windansea and Seadragon among them, are also bottled on their own. The house makes wines of other grapes, Albariño among them, but Pinot Noir is the grape it is known by. The Family Vineyards bottling makes the case for the upper valley: higher and more granitic than the valley below, it gives Pinot Noir of perfume and lift.

wine.name: Art of Chardonnay
wine.sites: One pocket of a single vineyard on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, where seams of quartz run through the clay.
wine.making: After whole bunch pressing, only the free run juice is fermented, mostly with wild yeast, in French oak barrels about a third new. The wine then rests on its lees for ten to eleven months through a full malolactic conversion, without stirring, and after a barrel selection it is bottled unfined and unfiltered.
wine.glass: Ripe lemon, lemon curd and a struck match note, with hazelnut and a gentle touch of cardamom; taut acidity carried on a creamy texture from the lees, and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Tight on release, it opens after three or four years and keeps for a decade from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's barrel selected Chardonnay from one pocket of a single vineyard, set at the head of its Chardonnays.

records.table: Chosen barrel by barrel from one pocket of quartz and clay on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, Art of Chardonnay heads the range at Creation, a house founded on unplanted land in 2002. Lemon curd, struck match and hazelnut lie over taut acidity; pour it cool, not cold.
records.story: Creation was founded in 2002 by a Swiss born winemaker and his South African born wife, of a Cape winemaking family, who bought land on the Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge that had never been planted to vines. Planting began in 2003, Pinot Noir among the first vines, from virus free material by the house's account. A small first harvest came in 2006, and the estate worked from its own cellar with the 2007 vintage, so that within about five years the bare slopes had become a wine farm. The Ridge is one of three wards that carry the Hemel-en-Aarde name. The house came to make four Chardonnays, the Estate, the Ridge, Glenn's and the Art of Chardonnay, and at their head it set the Art of Chardonnay, drawn from one pocket of a single vineyard where seams of quartz run through the clay, and chosen barrel by barrel. Glenn's Chardonnay comes from the same block, made apart, and the Art of Pinot Noir stands beside both. The wine is the youngest of the valley's Chardonnay stories, and its case is that a farm first planted in 2003 can give Chardonnay of grip and texture to set beside the older houses lower down.

wine.name: Hope Marguerite Chenin Blanc
wine.grapes: Chenin Blanc alone, from old vines.
wine.sites: The farm's two oldest Chenin Blanc blocks at Bot River, planted in 1974 and 1978.
wine.making: Fermented with its own wild yeasts in 400 litre French oak barrels, a small share of them new, and left on its gross lees for ten to eleven months with regular stirring before bottling.
wine.glass: Pear, white peach and lemon with honeysuckle and a flinty, struck note; a lean, taut palate with a gentle sweetness from the oak and a saline finish.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it gains honey and breadth over five to ten years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The name of a woman of the family, given to the house's barrel fermented old vine Chenin Blanc.
The Wine of Origin ward at the western gateway to Walker Bay, cooled by its lagoon.

records.table: From the farm's oldest blocks at Bot River, planted in 1974 and 1978, Beaumont makes Hope Marguerite, a barrel fermented Chenin Blanc. Pear, white peach and honeysuckle with a flinty edge make it lean and saline, a cool partner for fish.
records.story: The farm at Bot River, Compagnes Drift, began in the 1700s as an outpost of the Dutch East India Company, a supply farm for fruit, vegetables, dairy, wine and flour, and by the family's account it keeps a watermill of that century, among the oldest in South Africa. In 1974 the Beaumont family bought it, derelict, and set about replanting the vineyards; the two Chenin Blanc blocks that make Hope Marguerite date from 1974 and 1978. For years the farm's grapes went to the co-operative, until in 1994 the family left the co-operative system, refurbished the old cellar on the farm and made its first vintage under the Beaumont name. The first Hope Marguerite followed with the 1997 vintage, by the house's account: a barrel fermented Chenin Blanc named for the founding husband's late mother. The house also claims the first single varietal Mourvèdre bottled in South Africa, which Winemag reports, with a caution, for 1999. Hope Marguerite puts old Chenin Blanc at the centre of Bot River, the ward the Wines of South Africa body calls the gateway to Walker Bay, cooled by its lagoon and the bay, and reminds a guest that the district is more than Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

report: The plan's pick holds: the house and two retailers call Hope Marguerite its flagship white.
The purchase is 1974 by the house, the Bot River route and Broadbent; founded is 1974.
The first Hope Marguerite is 1997 by the house and a retailer; the Cape Winemakers Guild page says the Hope vineyard has fed it since 1996, so the story keeps 1997 as the house's account.
The namesake is the founding husband's late mother by the house and a second page; her dates were not found, so she is described, not dated, and only the label names her.
The founders and their son are not named; the son's taking of the cellar in 2004 and the family's step of 2015 were cut for want of two sources that agree.
The Mourvèdre claim rests on the house, Dreyfus Ashby and Winemag, which hedges it with apparently; it stays the house's claim.

changed: story: one of the oldest working watermills now a watermill of that century by the family's account, since one page says it is still working and another that it is being restored.
story: the step of 1994 now the co-operative left, the old cellar refurbished and the first vintage under the family name, as Dreyfus Ashby and the Bot River route tell it.
story: the namesake now the founding husband's late mother, as the house and a second page say, not the mother as most accounts tell it.
story: the Mourvèdre claim given Winemag's year of 1999 and its caution.
story: the son and his wife taking over in 2015 cut; the sources give the son's taking of the cellar in 2004 and nothing for 2015.
sources: Winemag's Hope Marguerite review replaced by Dreyfus Ashby, the source for 1994.
